newsitem.title: USA: Boeing, McDonnell Douglas in $13.3 billion merger.
newsitem.headline: Boeing, McDonnell Douglas in $13.3 billion merger.

text.p: The Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp said on Sunday they plan to merge, creating what they said would be the largest aerospace company in the world in a deal worth about $13.3 billion.

The combined firm, to operate under the Boeing Co name, was projected to have 1997 sales of about $48 billiion, with roughly $28 billion from Boeing and $20 billion from McDonnell Douglas, industry sources said.
Together, it would employ about 200,000 people and have a combined order backlog worth $100 billion.

The stock-for-stock merger, announced in a surprise news conference, will have huge implications for Airbus Industrie , the four-nation European consortium that is the other major player in the commercial aerospace industry.

Boeing and McDonnell Douglas said in a statement they had signed a definitive agreement under which McDonnell Douglas shareholders would receive 0.65 of a share of Boeing common stock for each share of McDonnell Douglas common share.
Based on Boeing's closing price of $96.75 on Friday, the companies said the deal would be worth about $13.3 billion.

Boeing chief executive Phil Condit told reporters he would serve as the combined company's chairman and chief executive, while McDonnell Douglas chief executive Harry Stonecipher would be its president and chief operating officer.
"I am here to announce that McDonnell Douglas will merge with Boeing in a stock for stock transaction," Condit told the news conference.
"The combination of these two companies are going to operate in the global marketplace as the Boeing Company and will be the world's leading aerospace company," he added.

Condit said he did not think the merger of the two, which is expected to take about six months to complete, would be "a big issue" on the antitrust front. He added that the firms had not yet had discussions with the government on whether it will grant antitrust approval.
Industry officials at the news conference said there would be some reassignments of personnel resulting from the merger, but said that they would seek to minimize any layoffs.

Boeing, based in Seattle, already has the leading position in the world commercial aircraft industry, historically holding a market share of about 50 percent and producing the 737, 747, 757, 767 and 777 airliners.
It also has major defense activities, making such products as the F-22 fighter and the Chinook and Comanche military helicopters.

St. Louis-based McDonnell Douglas is the third largest commercial aircraft company, and also makes a series of military aircraft, including the F/A-18 Hornet fighter, the C-17 Globemaster transport and the AH-64 Apache helicopter.
